summary:
Same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence in Gabon. The position has moved once in the opposite direction: the conduct was an offence from 5 July 2019 until its repeal in July 2020, and that episode is the clearest available guide to how quickly the legal position can shift. Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a colonial-era sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was not an offence at any point before 2019.

Criminalisation came with the new penal code, Law 042/2018, which entered into force on 5 July 2019. The statute did not name homosexuality. Article 402 listed "les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe" within the category of "atteintes aux mœurs", exposing those convicted to up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of five million CFA francs, reported as roughly US$8,500.

Enforcement was not theoretical. Two men were arrested within months of the code taking effect and were released only after paying police bribes, a sequence the US Department of State recorded in its 2019 human rights report on Gabon alongside documentation of societal discrimination. Gabon Review separately reported that police arrested two men alleged to be "gay marriers" in December 2013 and released them, an episode predating any statutory prohibition.

The ban was reversed in July 2020, when the National Assembly overturned the 2019 provision after Senate approval, restoring the pre-2019 position in which same-sex conduct was not criminal. The reversal sharply divided public opinion.

The constitution adopted by referendum on 16 November 2024, returning more than 90 per cent yes on roughly 55 per cent turnout, rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality. Article 18 codifies privacy protections relied on by LGBTI people, while Article 16 defines marriage in terms that exclude same-sex couples.

Legal gender recognition is not available, so a trans visitor's identity documents will stand as issued. Entry, visa and border-screening rules are not covered by the sources assembled here.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 constitution was drafted and ratified under the military regime that took power in the August 2023 coup, which ended 56 years of Bongo-family rule. The refusal to re-criminalise was therefore a choice made by an unelected government under pressure from civil-society campaigners, not the product of a settled legislative consensus, and the same document tightened the marriage definition.

Gabon's trajectory differs from the regional pattern in that no colonial-era sodomy law was ever on its books; the only period of criminalisation lasted thirteen months and was introduced by a domestic penal reform rather than inherited statute. That makes the 2019 to 2020 window the operative precedent for what a change of policy can produce here, including arrests within months of enactment.

Public opinion on the repeal remains divided, and the sources record no sustained enforcement of the 2019 provision beyond the two arrests. Comparable reporting on the region generally treats decriminalisation as stable where the legislature has affirmatively reversed a ban, but no monitoring data for Gabon post-2020 is present in this inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, so official documents continue to reflect sex assigned at registration and there is no procedure for amending them.

LGBTI organisations cannot register as legal entities, which limits formal advocacy, funding channels and any organised complaint machinery available to residents facing abuse.

Article 18 of the November 2024 constitution provides a privacy basis for challenging interference in consensual private conduct, while Article 16 fixes marriage as between a man and a woman, foreclosing partner recognition and the inheritance, hospital-visitation and residency rights attached to it.

The 2019 arrests involved police demanding bribes for release rather than a completed prosecution, which is the documented pattern residents can expect if enforcement pressure returns.
outOfScopeNotes:
The fine attached to the 2019 offence is reported inconsistently across sources, as five million CFA francs equating to roughly US$8,500 in one account and US$8,561 in another. The discrepancy is immaterial to the penalty's scale but is unresolved here.

Whether Article 402 was struck from the penal code text on repeal or left in place without application is not stated in the inventory; the sources establish only that the National Assembly overturned the 2019 ban.

No enforcement data, arrest figures or court decisions from Gabon after the July 2020 repeal are available in these sources, so the current practical treatment of same-sex conduct by police is not sourced.

The December 2013 arrest reported by Gabon Review has no stated outcome beyond release, and its legal basis at a time when no statute prohibited the conduct is not explained.

Nothing in the inventory addresses border screening, visa conditions, healthcare access or the safety of public facilities for trans visitors, so those areas remain not sourced rather than assessed.
